title: Linked list rewiring

why_it_exists.problem: We need to deeply manipulate the structure of a linked list (like reversing sublists, swapping nodes in pairs, or rotating). Re-creating the list wastes O(n) memory.
why_it_exists.naive_solution: Copy the values into an array, manipulate the array, and build a new linked list.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Manipulate the `next` pointers of the existing nodes directly in-place. Use a dummy head to handle edge cases easily.

mental_model.intuition: It's like unhooking train cars and hooking them up in a different order while the train is still on the tracks.
mental_model.description: Rewiring requires tracking multiple adjacent nodes (prev, curr, next). We carefully sever a `next` pointer and point it elsewhere, but we must save a reference to the severed tail first, or we lose the rest of the list.
mental_model.repeated_decision: Have I saved the reference to the next node before overwriting my current node's next pointer?

overview.what: Techniques for safely changing the `next` pointers of linked list nodes to achieve complex structural changes in O(1) space.
overview.why: It is the core mechanic behind all intermediate and advanced linked list interview questions.

why_learning_this: Pointer manipulation is a fundamental skill in systems programming (C/C++).
It rigorously tests your attention to detail and edge cases (like null pointers).

sections.body:
Rewiring a linked list is a dance of temporary variables. If you want node `A` to point to node `C` instead of `B`, you can write `A.next = C`. But if no other variable points to `B`, node `B` (and the rest of the list) is lost in memory. The golden rule of rewiring is: **always grab a reference to the next node before you break the link**.

For complex operations like Reversing a Sublist or Swapping Nodes in Pairs, we frequently use a `dummy` node. A dummy node is a fake head (`dummy = Node(0, head)`) that guarantees the list always has a node before the actual head. This eliminates the need for special `if head == target` branches when rewiring affects the first element.

When reversing a sublist (from position `m` to `n`), we first traverse to the node right before `m` (let's call it `prev`). Then, we do a standard reversal for `n - m` steps. Finally, we reconnect the broken ends: `prev` points to the new head of the reversed sublist, and the old head of the sublist points to the node right after `n`.

key_points.title: Dummy Head
key_points.detail: Always use a dummy head when the operation might change the head of the list. It turns edge cases into standard cases.

key_points.title: Temporary Pointers
key_points.detail: You almost always need `prev`, `curr`, and `nxt` pointers to safely rewire without orphans.

common_mistakes.title: Losing the rest of the list
common_mistakes.explanation: Overwriting `curr.next` before storing `curr.next` in a temporary variable orphans the remainder of the list, leading to a memory leak or wrong answer.

common_mistakes.title: Null pointer exceptions
common_mistakes.explanation: Trying to access `curr.next.next` without first checking if `curr` and `curr.next` are not `None`.

when_not_to_use.scenario: When read access speed is prioritized over memory
when_not_to_use.reason: If you need fast random access during the rewiring logic, copying to an array might be better in real systems, though it fails the O(1) space constraint of interviews.

failure_signals: You are using a `while` loop but getting a `NoneType has no attribute 'next'` error.

engineering_examples.title: OS Memory Management
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Free lists are often implemented as linked lists. Allocating and merging blocks involves complex rewiring of pointers.

recall_questions.q: Why is a dummy head node useful in linked list rewiring?
recall_questions.answer: It provides a guaranteed 'previous' node for the head, removing the need for special edge-case logic when the head itself is modified or deleted.

recall_questions.q: What is the golden rule of breaking a `next` pointer?
recall_questions.answer: Always store the `next` node in a temporary variable before overwriting the pointer, so you don't lose the rest of the list.

understanding_checks.question: If you write `curr.next = prev`, then `prev = curr`, then `curr = curr.next`, what happens to the traversal?
understanding_checks.answer: It goes backwards or enters an infinite loop.
understanding_checks.why: You just set `curr.next` to point backwards to `prev`. When you do `curr = curr.next`, you travel back to the node you just came from. You forgot to save the *original* `curr.next`.

understanding_checks.question: What is the space complexity of reversing a sublist of length M in a linked list of length N?
understanding_checks.why: We only use a few constant pointers (prev, curr, nxt), regardless of the length of the list.

oa_questions.question: Swap Nodes in Pairs
oa_questions.answer: Use a dummy head. Iterate in steps of 2, rewiring `prev.next`, `curr.next`, and `nxt.next`.
oa_questions.approach: Draw out the 3 pointers before coding. Save `curr.next.next`.

practice_tasks.title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
practice_tasks.prompt: Given a linked list, swap every two adjacent nodes and return its head. You must solve the problem without modifying the values in the list's nodes.
practice_tasks.solution:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
def swapPairs(head):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    curr = head
    while curr and curr.next:
        nxt_pair = curr.next.next
        second = curr.next
        second.next = curr
        curr.next = nxt_pair
        prev.next = second
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt_pair
    return dummy.next
